newsitem.title: INDIA: India launches tax amnesty to mop up black money.
newsitem.headline: India launches tax amnesty to mop up black money.

text.p: The Indian government on Wednesday launched a tax amnesty scheme to take in more revenues and combat black money, but said collectors would crack down on tax dodgers after the plan closes in six months.

Officials said the Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme (VDIS), which had been broadly outlined in the 1997/98 (April-March) budget presented on February 28, would begin on July 1 and end on December 31.
The six-month scheme aims to draw tax evaders who operate in the shadows of the "parallel economy" into the tax net.
Private economists say at least four of every 10 rupees earned in India are generated in the black economy and are never declared to authorities.
Ravi Kant, chairman of the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), told a news conference: "We want 100 percent integration of the parallel economy with the mainstream."
But he refused to put a figure on the size of the black economy. "We do not want to hazard a guess," he said.
The scheme offers tax evaders, even those under investigation under the Foreign Exchange Regulations Act (FERA), the opportunity to come clean without penalty.
But the VDIS bars people who have been detained under FERA from taking advantage of the scheme, raising some eyebrows.

"It is something very difficult to understand. What will happen to people who have been detained under FERA and not proven guilty?" V. Raghuraman, secretary general of Associated Chambers of Commerce (Assocham), told Reuters.
The Finance Ministry has launched a media blitz to highlight the scheme and hired a private public relations firm.

In the budget he presented to parliament in February, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram slashed the tax rate for the highest personal income bracket to 30 percent from 40, and the corporate tax rate to 35 percent from 40 in the 1997/98 budget.
"The government needs to get 300 to 400 billion rupees ($8.4 billion to $11 billion) to come in through this scheme or else it would serve no purpose," Raghuraman said.
Officials cautioned that VDIS offered the last chance for tax evaders to come clean. "We do not really expect the need for these schemes in the future," Kant said.

Of the money raised through the scheme, 77.5 percent will go to the states and the balance will remain with the federal government. The money will be used to develop infrastructure, as well as health and education projects throughout the country.
